```{r}
source("_common.R")
```

# Journal Entry Testing {#sec-jet}

A State warehousing corporation keeps its accounts on an ERP system. Every bill, receipt, salary run and depreciation charge reaches the general ledger as a journal entry. Most entries are made by the system itself, or keyed in by the accountants as part of their daily work. A few are different. A manager books a large sum as income on the last day of the year. A store keeper, who has no business in the ledger, posts bills late at night. An accountant keeps every bill just below the amount that needs the General Manager's approval. Each of these entries looks ordinary on its own. Among twenty thousand others, nobody notices them.

Journal entries are where management can **override controls**. A person with enough authority can record an entry that no ordinary control will stop, because the controls are run by the same people. Standards on auditing therefore single out journal entries for testing. This chapter shows how to test every entry in a general ledger with R, rather than a handful picked by hand.

This chapter opens Part IX, which applies the techniques of earlier chapters to whole audit areas. The chapters after it do the same for tenders. We will check that the ledger received is complete. We will profile who posts, when and to which accounts. We will then run one test for each characteristic of a suspicious entry, using dates and times (@sec-lubridate), round numbers and approval limits (@sec-nigrini), duplicates (@sec-dup), narrations (@sec-text-je), segregation of duties (@sec-process-sod) and rare combinations (@sec-apriori). Finally we will combine the tests into a simple risk score, in the spirit of @sec-tenderflags-cri, and select entries for examination.

As with every chapter in this part, a flag is not a finding. Most flagged entries will have a good reason. The aim is to find the few that need a question, and to show in the working papers why those were chosen.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Why journal entries matter {#sec-jet-why}

The standards on auditing that deal with fraud are SA 240, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, and ISA 240, its international counterpart. Both recognise that management is in a unique position to commit fraud by overriding controls. So, whatever the auditor's view of the risk, both require procedures to test the appropriateness of journal entries recorded in the general ledger, and of other adjustments made in preparing the financial statements. The auditor is expected to select entries made at the end of the reporting period, and to consider entries made throughout the period. The standards also ask the auditor to understand the entity's process for making entries, and to talk to the people who make them.

Auditing guidance describes the features that fraudulent entries often have. They are general characteristics, not rules, and each of them also fits many honest entries. The table below lists them, with the test this chapter uses for each.

| Characteristic | Test in this chapter |
|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Recorded at the end of the period, or after closing | @sec-jet-late |
| Made by people who do not normally make entries | @sec-jet-users |
| Made at unusual times | @sec-jet-hours |
| Approved by the same person who made them | @sec-jet-self |
| Amounts just below an approval limit | @sec-jet-limit |
| Round amounts, or amounts with the same endings | @sec-jet-round |
| Little or no explanation | @sec-jet-narration |
| The same entry posted twice | @sec-jet-dup |
| Reversed soon after the period end | @sec-jet-reversed |
| Manual entries to revenue or cash | @sec-jet-revcash |
| Unrelated, unusual or seldom-used accounts | @sec-jet-pairs |

: Characteristics of suspicious journal entries, and the tests that look for them {#tbl-jet-characteristics}

The same question arises in Indian government audit wherever accounts are kept on the commercial pattern. Public sector undertakings, autonomous bodies and corporations increasingly run ERP systems, whose ledgers can be extracted in full. Testing every entry is then quicker than testing a sample. It also shows patterns that a sample cannot, such as one user's entries clustering below a limit.

## Our data, a general ledger of a State warehousing company {#sec-jet-data}

Our auditee is an imaginary State warehousing corporation. It stores foodgrains and other goods for depositors, earns storage and handling charges, and is building new godowns. We have received its general ledger for 2024-25, and for April and May 2025, the months in which the accounts were closed.

The table `gl` has one row for each line of a journal entry, with these columns.

- `je_id` is the entry number, and `line` the line within the entry. Every entry has two or more lines.
- `fy` and `period` give the financial year and the month within it. April is period 1 and March is period 12. Entries dated 31 March but recorded after the year end go to a special **period 13**, which the ERP keeps for year-end adjustments.
- `posting_date` is the accounting date, and `document_date` the date of the bill or voucher behind it. `entered_at` is the date and time when the entry was actually keyed in, in Indian Standard Time.
- `account_code`, `account_name` and `account_type` (Asset, Liability, Income or Expense) identify the account.
- `debit` and `credit` are the amounts, in rupees. On each line, one of them is zero.
- `source` is "System" for entries made by an interface, such as billing or payroll, and "Manual" for entries keyed in by a person.
- `user_id` is the person who made the entry, and `approver_id` the person who approved it. System entries have no approver.
- `narration` is the explanation typed with the entry.

There are also four smaller tables. `coa` is the chart of accounts. `users` is the user master, with each user's department, role, and dates of joining and leaving. `tb` is the trial balance for 2024-25, printed from the ERP. `holidays` lists the gazetted holidays of the State. The company works Monday to Friday.

The company's own rules, which we will test against, are simple. A manual entry above ₹10 lakh must be approved by the General Manager (Finance). Smaller entries are approved by one of the two Managers (Finance). Every manual entry above ₹1 lakh must be approved by someone other than the person who made it.

Most of the ledger is routine. The billing interface posts storage bills every night, and bank receipts are imported each morning. The system posts payroll and depreciation at month end. Accountants book provisions on the last working day of each month, and the system reverses them the next day. The accountants worked over the closing weekend in March. After the year end, the finance team booked genuine provisions, and late bills of March were entered in April. Eight cases have been planted.

1. **A year-end revenue boost.** A manager books six entries of storage income, dated 31 March 2025 but keyed in during April. They debit receivables and credit revenue. In May they are reversed.
2. **A user who should not be posting.** A store keeper posts bills of one vendor, often late at night or on holidays.
3. **Self-approved entries.** A manager approves their own entries above ₹1 lakh.
4. **Entries just below the approval limit.** One accountant keeps keying in bills a little under ₹10 lakh.
5. **Round amounts to suspense and provisions.** Round sums are moved to the suspense account, and round provisions for repairs are booked in March.
6. **A rare account combination.** Capital work-in-progress is paid in cash, three times.
7. **Narrations that explain nothing.** A dozen entries say only "adj", "ok" or "as per instructions", or nothing at all.
8. **A duplicate.** One vendor's bill is posted twice, two days apart.

The extract also has a problem of completeness, which we must find before running any test.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code to create the general ledger"
set.seed(2425)

# Gazetted holidays of the imaginary State, and the company's working days (Monday to Friday)
holidays <- as.Date(c("2024-04-11", "2024-04-17", "2024-05-23", "2024-08-15", "2024-08-26",
                      "2024-10-02", "2024-10-31", "2024-11-15", "2024-12-25", "2025-01-26",
                      "2025-02-26", "2025-03-14", "2025-04-18", "2025-05-12"))
all_days <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-05-31"), by = "day")
work_days <- all_days[wday(all_days, week_start = 1) <= 5 & !all_days %in% holidays]
next_wd <- function(d) work_days[pmin(findInterval(as.numeric(d) - 1, as.numeric(work_days)) + 1,
                                      length(work_days))]
stamp <- function(d, h) force_tz(as_datetime(d), "Asia/Kolkata") + round(h * 3600)
office_h <- function(n) pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 13.8, 2), 9.7), 18.6)
fy_wd <- work_days[work_days <= as.Date("2025-03-31")]

coa <- tribble(
  ~account_code, ~account_name,                      ~account_type,
  "1101",        "Cash in hand",                     "Asset",
  "1102",        "Bank current account",             "Asset",
  "1201",        "Trade receivables",                "Asset",
  "1301",        "Advances to staff",                "Asset",
  "1401",        "Capital work-in-progress",         "Asset",
  "1501",        "Buildings and warehouses",         "Asset",
  "1502",        "Accumulated depreciation",         "Asset",
  "1601",        "Suspense account",                 "Asset",
  "1701",        "GST input credit",                 "Asset",
  "2101",        "Trade payables",                   "Liability",
  "2201",        "Salary payable",                   "Liability",
  "2301",        "TDS payable",                      "Liability",
  "2302",        "GST output payable",               "Liability",
  "2401",        "Provision for expenses",           "Liability",
  "2402",        "Provision for doubtful debts",     "Liability",
  "2403",        "Provision for gratuity",           "Liability",
  "2501",        "Security deposits from depositors", "Liability",
  "3101",        "Storage charges",                  "Income",
  "3102",        "Handling charges",                 "Income",
  "3201",        "Interest income",                  "Income",
  "3301",        "Miscellaneous income",             "Income",
  "4101",        "Salaries and wages",               "Expense",
  "4102",        "Gratuity expense",                 "Expense",
  "4201",        "Electricity",                      "Expense",
  "4202",        "Repairs and maintenance",          "Expense",
  "4203",        "Security services",                "Expense",
  "4204",        "Fumigation and chemicals",         "Expense",
  "4301",        "Depreciation",                     "Expense",
  "4401",        "Office expenses",                  "Expense",
  "4402",        "Audit fee",                        "Expense",
  "4501",        "Bad and doubtful debts",           "Expense"
)
acc_label <- c("4201" = "electricity", "4202" = "repairs of godowns", "4203" = "security services",
               "4204" = "fumigation chemicals", "4401" = "office expenses")

users <- tribble(
  ~user_id, ~department,              ~role,                       ~joined,      ~left,
  "ACC01",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2016-07-01", NA,
  "ACC02",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2018-03-12", NA,
  "ACC03",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2019-08-01", NA,
  "ACC04",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2021-01-04", NA,
  "ACC05",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2022-06-15", NA,
  "ACC06",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2025-01-01", NA,
  "ACC07",  "Accounts",               "Accountant",                "2012-04-02", "2024-12-31",
  "ACM01",  "Accounts",               "Manager (Finance)",         "2010-09-01", NA,
  "ACM02",  "Accounts",               "Manager (Finance)",         "2014-02-17", NA,
  "FIN01",  "Finance",                "General Manager (Finance)", "2008-05-05", NA,
  "HR01",   "Human Resources",        "Payroll officer",           "2017-11-20", NA,
  "ITA02",  "Information Technology", "System administrator",      "2020-10-01", NA,
  "STR03",  "Stores",                 "Store keeper",              "2019-02-11", NA,
  "SYSTEM", "Information Technology", "Batch interface",           NA,           NA
) |>
  mutate(across(c(joined, left), as.Date))

acc_for <- function(d) {
  sixth <- if_else(d <= as.Date("2024-12-31"), "ACC07", "ACC06")
  pick <- sample(1:6, length(d), TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.18, 0.14, 0.14, 0.14))
  if_else(pick == 6, sixth, sprintf("ACC%02d", pick))
}
approver_for <- function(amount) {
  if_else(amount > 1e6, "FIN01", sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), length(amount), TRUE))
}

# Entries are collected in E and their lines in L
E <- list(); L <- list(); k <- 0
keys <- function(n) { k <<- k + n; seq_len(n) + k - n }
dr <- function(e, acc, amt) tibble(key = e$key, account_code = acc, debit = amt, credit = 0)
cr <- function(e, acc, amt) tibble(key = e$key, account_code = acc, debit = 0, credit = amt)
add <- function(e, lines, case = NA_character_) {
  E[[length(E) + 1]] <<- mutate(e, case = case)
  L[[length(L) + 1]] <<- lines
}
entry <- function(d, entered, source, user, approver, narration, doc = d) {
  tibble(key = keys(length(d)), posting_date = d, document_date = doc, entered_at = entered,
         source = source, user_id = user, approver_id = approver, narration = narration)
}

# 1. Storage bills, posted every night by the billing interface
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 16)); n <- length(d)
storage <- round(rlnorm(n, log(110000), 0.8), 2)
handling <- if_else(runif(n) < 0.3, round(rlnorm(n, log(25000), 0.6), 2), 0)
gst <- round(0.18 * (storage + handling), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 23 + runif(n, 0, 0.9)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Storage bill SB/", sample(10000:99999, n, TRUE), " to depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1201", storage + handling + gst), cr(e, "3101", storage),
                 cr(e[handling > 0, ], "3102", handling[handling > 0]), cr(e, "2302", gst)))

# 2. Receipts from depositors, imported from the bank statement each morning
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 15)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(120000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10, 10.8)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Receipt from depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE), ", UTR ", sample(1e8:9e8, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)))

# 3. Vendor bills keyed in by the accountants
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 10)); n <- length(d)
base <- round(rlnorm(n, log(45000), 1.1), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
exp_acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.35, 0.2, 0.25))
ent_d <- next_wd(d + if_else(runif(n) < 0.3, sample(1:3, n, TRUE), 0L))
e <- entry(d, stamp(ent_d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, n, TRUE), " of vendor V-",
                  sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, n, TRUE)), " for ", acc_label[exp_acc]),
           doc = d - sample(0:20, n, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, exp_acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))

# 4. Payments to vendors
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 9)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(52000), 1.1), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Payment to vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, n, TRUE)),
                  " against bill no ", sample(100:9999, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2101", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))

# 5. Petty cash. Many small round amounts, and a few entries keyed in without a narration
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 2)); n <- length(d)
amt <- if_else(runif(n) < 0.5, sample(c(500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 5000), n, TRUE),
               round(runif(n, 200, 9000)))
narr <- paste0("Petty cash, ", sample(c("tea and refreshments", "courier charges", "local conveyance",
                                         "stationery", "minor repairs to furniture"), n, TRUE))
narr[sample(n, 6)] <- ""
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE), narr)
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", amt), cr(e, "1101", amt)))

# 6. Cash drawn from the bank every Monday
d <- work_days[wday(work_days, week_start = 1) == 1]; n <- length(d)
amt <- sample(c(20000, 25000, 30000), n, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10.5, 12)), "Manual", "ACC03", "ACM01",
           paste0("Cash drawn for petty expenses, cheque no ", sample(400000:499999, n)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1101", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))

# 7. Advances to staff, and their adjustment against bills a few weeks later
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 1)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(runif(n, 5000, 50000), -3)
emp <- sprintf("E-%03d", sample(1:350, n, TRUE))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           paste0("Advance to employee ", emp, " for tour"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1301", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(10:40, n, TRUE)); keep <- d2 > d
adj <- round(amt * runif(n, 0.7, 1), 2)
e <- entry(d2[keep], stamp(d2[keep], office_h(sum(keep))), "Manual", acc_for(d2[keep]),
           sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), sum(keep), TRUE),
           paste0("Tour advance of ", emp[keep], " adjusted against TA bill"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", adj[keep]), cr(e, "1301", adj[keep])))

# 8. Running bills of contractors building new godowns, and capitalisation on completion
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 0.5)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(600000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Being RA bill no ", sample(1:12, n, TRUE), " of contractor V-",
                  sample(c("041", "057", "063"), n, TRUE), " for construction of godown"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1401", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)))
d <- as.Date(c("2024-09-30", "2024-12-31", "2025-03-28")); amt <- c(21000000, 14000000, 33000000)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, c(15.5, 16.2, 15.1)), "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01",
           paste("Capitalisation of godown at", c("Rampur", "Keshavnagar", "Sitapur"), "on completion"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1501", amt), cr(e, "1401", amt)))

# 9. Security deposits received from depositors
d <- rep(fy_wd, rpois(length(fy_wd), 0.7)); n <- length(d)
amt <- sample(c(25000, 50000, 75000, 100000, 150000, 200000), n, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), approver_for(amt),
           paste0("Security deposit received from depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "2501", amt)))

# 10. Interest on deposits, each quarter, and small miscellaneous income
d <- as.Date(c("2024-06-28", "2024-09-30", "2024-12-31", "2025-03-28")); n <- 4
amt <- round(runif(n, 1800000, 2500000), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", "ACC02", "FIN01", "Interest on fixed deposits for the quarter")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "3201", amt)))
d <- rep(work_days, rpois(length(work_days), 0.1)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(15000), 0.8), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           sample(c("Sale of tender forms", "Sale of scrap gunny bags", "Penalty recovered from depositor"), n, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "3301", amt)))

# 11. Unidentified bank receipts parked in suspense, and cleared when the depositor is known
d <- rep(fy_wd, rpois(length(fy_wd), 0.3)); n <- length(d)
amt <- round(rlnorm(n, log(80000), 0.7), 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, runif(n, 10, 10.8)), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
           paste0("Unidentified credit in bank, UTR ", sample(1e8:9e8, n)))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1102", amt), cr(e, "1601", amt)))
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(5:40, n, TRUE))
e <- entry(d2, stamp(d2, office_h(n)), "Manual", acc_for(d2), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), n, TRUE),
           paste0("Unidentified receipt cleared, depositor D-", sample(100:480, n, TRUE), " identified"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1601", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)))

# 12. Monthly postings. Payroll, statutory dues, depreciation, rent of security, accruals
godowns <- c("Rampur", "Keshavnagar", "Sitapur", "Bhawanipur", "Chandgarh", "Dhanpur",
             "Madhopur", "Ratanpur")
months_list <- seq(as.Date("2024-04-01"), as.Date("2025-05-01"), by = "month")
for (i in seq_along(months_list)) {
  m <- months_list[i]
  wd_m <- work_days[work_days >= m & work_days < m %m+% months(1)]
  last_day <- m %m+% months(1) - 1
  gross <- round(rnorm(1, 16200000, 300000), 2); tds <- round(0.08 * gross, 2)
  e <- entry(max(wd_m), stamp(max(wd_m), 20.5), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
             paste("Salary for", format(m, "%B %Y"), "from payroll"))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4101", gross), cr(e, "2201", gross - tds), cr(e, "2301", tds)))
  e <- entry(last_day, stamp(last_day, 23.8), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
             paste("Depreciation for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4301", 1842300), cr(e, "1502", 1842300)))
  sec_d <- wd_m[4]
  e <- entry(sec_d, stamp(sec_d, office_h(1)), "Manual", "ACC02", "ACM01",
             paste("Being bill of vendor V-012 for security services,", format(m, "%B %Y")))
  add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4203", 385000), dr(e, "1701", 69300), cr(e, "2101", 454300)))
  if (i < length(months_list)) {
    wd_next <- work_days[work_days >= m %m+% months(1) & work_days < m %m+% months(2)]
    e <- entry(wd_next[1], stamp(wd_next[1], 11.5), "Manual", "ACC01", "FIN01",
               paste("Salary paid for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2201", gross - tds), cr(e, "1102", gross - tds)))
    d7 <- next_wd(m %m+% months(1) + 5)
    e <- entry(d7, stamp(d7, 12.5), "Manual", "ACC02", "FIN01", paste("TDS deposited for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2301", tds), cr(e, "1102", tds)))
    d20 <- next_wd(m %m+% months(1) + 18); gst_amt <- round(rnorm(1, 9000000, 900000), 2)
    e <- entry(d20, stamp(d20, 15), "Manual", "ACC03", "FIN01", paste("GST paid for", format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2302", gst_amt), cr(e, "1102", gst_amt)))
    # Month-end accruals, reversed automatically on the first day of the next month
    acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 8, TRUE)
    amt <- round(rlnorm(8, log(150000), 0.6), -4)
    gd <- sample(godowns)
    e <- entry(rep(max(wd_m), 8), stamp(max(wd_m), runif(8, 15, 18)), "Manual",
               sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02"), 8, TRUE), sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), 8, TRUE),
               paste0("Being provision for ", acc_label[acc], " at ", gd, " godown for ",
                      format(m, "%B %Y"), ", bill awaited"))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, amt), cr(e, "2401", amt)))
    first_day <- m %m+% months(1)
    e <- entry(rep(first_day, 8), stamp(first_day, 0.3), "System", "SYSTEM", NA,
               paste0("Auto reversal of provision for ", acc_label[acc], " at ", gd, " godown for ",
                      format(m, "%B %Y")))
    add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2401", amt), cr(e, acc, amt)))
  }
}

# 13. Payroll corrections by the payroll officer, and two test entries by the system administrator
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd, 12)); amt <- round(runif(12, 5000, 60000))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(12)), "Manual", "HR01", "ACM01",
           paste0("Arrears of DA to employee E-", sample(100:350, 12), ", payroll correction"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4101", amt), cr(e, "2201", amt)))
d <- as.Date("2024-08-17")
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 15.2), "Manual", "ITA02", "ITA02", "Test entry after ERP patch")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", 1), cr(e, "1101", 1)))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 15.4), "Manual", "ITA02", "ITA02", "Reversal of test entry after ERP patch")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1101", 1), cr(e, "4401", 1)))

# 14. Genuine year-end work. Bills keyed in over the closing weekend, late bills for March
#     entered in April, and year-end provisions by the finance team
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-28"), 20)
ent <- stamp(as.Date("2025-03-29") + rep(0:1, each = 10), runif(20, 10.5, 17.5))
base <- round(rlnorm(20, log(60000), 0.9), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 20, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, ent, "Manual", sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02", "ACC03"), 20, TRUE), approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 20), " of vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, 20)),
                  " for ", acc_label[acc]), doc = d - sample(0:10, 20, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 15)
ent_d <- sort(sample(work_days[work_days >= as.Date("2025-04-01") & work_days <= as.Date("2025-04-25")], 15, TRUE))
base <- round(rlnorm(15, log(80000), 0.9), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
acc <- sample(c("4201", "4202", "4204", "4401"), 15, TRUE)
e <- entry(d, stamp(ent_d, office_h(15)), "Manual", sample(c("ACC01", "ACC02"), 15, TRUE),
           approver_for(base + gst),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 15), " of vendor V-", sprintf("%03d", sample(1:180, 15)),
                  " for ", acc_label[acc], ", March 2025, received late"),
           doc = as.Date("2025-03-31") - sample(0:20, 15, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, acc, base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)))
d <- rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 3)
e <- entry(d, stamp(as.Date(c("2025-04-22", "2025-04-24", "2025-04-15")), c(11.5, 16.2, 12)),
           "Manual", c("FIN01", "FIN01", "ACM01"), c("FIN01", "FIN01", "FIN01"),
           c("Provision for gratuity as per actuarial valuation report dated 18.04.2025",
             "Provision for doubtful debts on receivables over three years old, as per Board note",
             "Provision for statutory audit fee for 2024-25"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, c("4102", "4501", "4402"), c(3846215, 6240000, 300000)),
                 cr(e, c("2403", "2402", "2401"), c(3846215, 6240000, 300000))))

# ---- Planted cases ----
# Planted 1. Storage income booked on 31 March 2025, entered in April, reversed in May
amt <- c(4860000, 5230000, 3975000, 6120000, 4490000, 5540000)
e <- entry(rep(as.Date("2025-03-31"), 6),
           stamp(as.Date(c("2025-04-09", "2025-04-10", "2025-04-11", "2025-04-12", "2025-04-12", "2025-04-12")),
                 c(18.8, 17.6, 19.3, 11.1, 11.7, 12.2)),
           "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01", "Storage income for March 2025, bills under preparation")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1201", amt), cr(e, "3101", amt)), "1 Revenue boost")
d <- as.Date(c("2025-05-07", "2025-05-07", "2025-05-08", "2025-05-08", "2025-05-09", "2025-05-09"))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(6)), "Manual", "ACM01", "FIN01", "Rectification of entry dated 31.03.2025")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "3101", amt), cr(e, "1201", amt)), "1 Revenue boost reversal")

# Planted 2. A store keeper posts bills of one vendor, often at night or on holidays
ent <- ymd_hm(c("2024-07-09 22:40", "2024-08-15 12:15", "2024-08-29 23:05", "2024-09-21 16:30",
                "2024-10-02 11:50", "2024-10-24 00:45", "2024-11-12 15:20", "2024-11-28 22:55",
                "2024-12-25 13:10", "2025-01-14 23:30", "2025-01-26 12:40", "2025-02-06 15:05",
                "2025-02-20 00:20", "2025-03-08 17:45"), tz = "Asia/Kolkata")
d <- as_date(ent - hours(2)); base <- round(rlnorm(14, log(320000), 0.35), 2); gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
bill_no <- sample(2000:2999, 14)
e <- entry(d, ent, "Manual", "STR03", "ACM02",
           paste0("Being bill no ", bill_no, " of vendor V-217 for fumigation chemicals"),
           doc = d - sample(2:10, 14, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4204", base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)), "2 Store keeper")
d2 <- next_wd(d + sample(12:25, 14, TRUE))
e <- entry(d2, stamp(d2, office_h(14)), "Manual", acc_for(d2), "ACM02",
           paste0("Payment to vendor V-217 against bill no ", bill_no))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "2101", base + gst), cr(e, "1102", base + gst)))

# Planted 3. A manager approves their own entries above Rs 1 lakh
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd[fy_wd >= as.Date("2024-06-01")], 8)); base <- round(runif(8, 150000, 720000), 2)
gst <- round(0.18 * base, 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(8)), "Manual", "ACM02", "ACM02",
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 8), " of vendor V-1", sample(10:99, 8),
                  " for repairs of godown no G-", sample(10:60, 8)), doc = d - sample(1:15, 8, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", base), dr(e, "1701", gst), cr(e, "2101", base + gst)), "3 Self-approved")

# Planted 4. Bills just below the approval limit of Rs 10 lakh, all keyed in by one accountant
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd[fy_wd >= as.Date("2024-09-01")], 22)); tot <- round(runif(22, 955000, 999000), 2)
base <- round(tot / 1.18, 2)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(22)), "Manual", "ACC04", sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), 22, TRUE),
           paste0("Being bill no ", sample(100:9999, 22), " of vendor V-", sample(c("131", "142", "158"), 22, TRUE),
                  " for repairs of godowns"), doc = d - sample(1:15, 22, TRUE))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", base), dr(e, "1701", tot - base), cr(e, "2101", tot)), "4 Below limit")

# Planted 5. Round amounts sent to suspense, and round provisions for repairs in March
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd[fy_wd >= as.Date("2024-10-01")], 6))
amt <- c(200000, 500000, 300000, 750000, 400000, 250000)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(6)), "Manual", "ACC05", "ACM02", "Amount transferred to suspense, to be adjusted")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1601", amt), cr(e, "1102", amt)), "5 Round to suspense")
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd[fy_wd >= as.Date("2025-03-03")], 4)); amt <- c(500000, 800000, 600000, 900000)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(4)), "Manual", "ACC05", "ACM01", "Provision for repairs")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", amt), cr(e, "2401", amt)), "5 Round to provision")

# Planted 6. Capital work paid in cash
d <- as.Date(c("2024-10-22", "2025-01-09", "2025-03-19")); amt <- c(184500, 226000, 197300)
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(3)), "Manual", "ACC02", "ACM01", "Payment to contractor for godown shed work")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "1401", amt), cr(e, "1101", amt)), "6 Rare pair")

# Planted 7. Narrations that explain nothing
d <- sort(sample(fy_wd, 12)); amt <- round(runif(12, 40000, 400000), 2)
usr <- sample(c(rep("ACC05", 8), "ACC03", "ACC03", "ACC07", "ACC07"))
usr[usr == "ACC07" & d > as.Date("2024-12-31")] <- "ACC06"
dra <- rep(c("4401", "4202", "1301"), each = 4); cra <- "2401"
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, office_h(12)), "Manual", usr, sample(c("ACM01", "ACM02"), 12, TRUE),
           c("", "adj", "as per instructions", "ok", "jv", "", "adj", "as per instructions",
             "adjustment", "..", "as per instructions", "adj"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, dra, amt), cr(e, cra, amt)), "7 Narration")

# Planted 8. The same bill posted twice, two days apart
d <- as.Date(c("2025-02-11", "2025-02-13"))
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, c(12.4, 16.1)), "Manual", "ACC06", "ACM01",
           "Being bill no 1187 of vendor V-088 for repairs of godown roof", doc = as.Date("2025-02-05"))
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4202", 370779.66), dr(e, "1701", 66740.34), cr(e, "2101", 437520)), "8 Duplicate")

# An entry that is in the trial balance but will be missing from the extract
d <- as.Date("2024-11-19")
e <- entry(d, stamp(d, 14.33), "Manual", "ACC03", "ACM02", "Purchase of printer cartridges, cash memo 4471")
add(e, bind_rows(dr(e, "4401", 46850), cr(e, "1101", 46850)), "Missing")

# ---- Assemble the ledger ----
entries <- bind_rows(E) |>
  arrange(entered_at, key) |>
  mutate(je_id = sprintf("JE%06d", 100000 + row_number()),
         fy = if_else(posting_date <= as.Date("2025-03-31"), "2024-25", "2025-26"),
         period = (month(posting_date) - 4) %% 12 + 1,
         period = if_else(posting_date == as.Date("2025-03-31") &
                            as_date(entered_at) > as.Date("2025-03-31"), 13, period))

gl_all <- bind_rows(L) |>
  filter(debit > 0 | credit > 0) |>
  inner_join(entries, by = "key") |>
  arrange(je_id, desc(debit)) |>
  mutate(line = row_number(), .by = je_id) |>
  left_join(coa, by = "account_code") |>
  select(je_id, line, fy, period, posting_date, document_date, entered_at, account_code,
         account_name, account_type, debit, credit, source, user_id, approver_id, narration)

# The trial balance printed from the ERP, for 2024-25
tb <- gl_all |>
  filter(fy == "2024-25") |>
  summarise(debit = sum(debit), credit = sum(credit), .by = account_code) |>
  right_join(coa, by = "account_code") |>
  mutate(across(c(debit, credit), \(x) round(coalesce(x, 0), 2))) |>
  select(account_code, account_name, debit, credit) |>
  arrange(account_code)

planted <- entries |>
  filter(!is.na(case)) |>
  select(je_id, case)

# The extract received by the auditor lacks one entry
gl <- gl_all |>
  filter(!je_id %in% planted$je_id[planted$case == "Missing"])

rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c("gl", "coa", "users", "tb", "holidays", "planted")))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
crore <- function(x) round(x / 1e7, 2)
lakh <- function(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)
inr <- function(x) {
  s <- as.character(round(x))
  vapply(s, function(v) {
    n <- nchar(v)
    if (n <= 3) return(v)
    head <- gsub("(\\d)(?=(\\d{2})+$)", "\\1,", substr(v, 1, n - 3), perl = TRUE)
    paste0(head, ",", substr(v, n - 2, n))
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

Let us look at the ledger.

```{r}
glimpse(gl)
```

```{r}
users
```

The ledger has `r big(nrow(gl))` lines in `r big(n_distinct(gl$je_id))` entries. Before any test, though, we must make sure that it is the whole ledger.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, asking for the ledger

Ask for the **full** general ledger for the year and the closing months, not a report filtered by someone else. It should have one row per line, with the entry number, posting date, document date, date and time of entry, source, maker, approver and narration. Ask also for the user master, the chart of accounts and the trial balance of the same date, printed by the ERP. Note who ran the extract, when, and with which query, so that it can be run again. The ledger must reconcile to the trial balance before any test. Handling such data safely is covered in @sec-privacy.
:::

## From lines to entries {#sec-jet-entries}

The ledger has one row per line, but most tests are about whole entries. Who made the entry, when, and for how much? So we first make a second table with one row per entry. Let us see the idea on two tiny entries. The first is a bill with GST, and the second a receipt.

```{r}
tiny <- tribble(
  ~je_id, ~account_code, ~debit, ~credit,
  "JE1",  "4202",        50000,  0,
  "JE1",  "1701",        9000,   0,
  "JE1",  "2101",        0,      59000,
  "JE2",  "1102",        20000,  0,
  "JE2",  "1201",        0,      20000
)

tiny |>
  summarise(lines = n(), debit = sum(debit), credit = sum(credit), .by = je_id)
```

`summarise(.by = je_id)` gives one row per entry. In a balanced entry, the total debit equals the total credit, so either of them is the **amount** of the entry. Now for the whole ledger. The columns that are the same on every line of an entry go into `.by`, so that they are kept.

```{r}
je <- gl |>
  summarise(amount = sum(debit), lines = n(),
            .by = c(je_id, fy, period, posting_date, document_date, entered_at,
                    source, user_id, approver_id, narration))

je
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_je <- nrow(je)
n_manual <- sum(je$source == "Manual")
```

There are `r big(n_je)` entries. `r big(n_manual)` of them are manual, and the rest come from the system.

## First, is the ledger complete? {#sec-jet-complete}

A journal entry test looks for entries that should not be there. It cannot find entries that are missing from the data we were given. If the extract leaves out some entries, every test that follows is run on the wrong population. A clean result would prove nothing. So the first checks are about the data itself.

### Every entry balances

Each entry must have equal debits and credits. Let us check all of them. We compare with a small tolerance, because sums of amounts with paise can differ in the last decimal place inside the computer.

```{r}
gl |>
  summarise(debit = sum(debit), credit = sum(credit), .by = je_id) |>
  filter(abs(debit - credit) > 0.005)
```

No entry is out of balance. This is what we expect from an ERP. An entry that does not balance would mean the extract was cut in the middle of an entry, or that lines were lost.

### The ledger agrees with the trial balance

Next, the total debits and credits of each account in the ledger should equal those in the trial balance. Our trial balance shows the debits and credits of each account during 2024-25. We total the ledger in the same way, and join the two.

```{r}
ledger_totals <- gl |>
  filter(fy == "2024-25") |>
  summarise(gl_debit = sum(debit), gl_credit = sum(credit), .by = account_code)

tb_check <- tb |>
  left_join(ledger_totals, by = "account_code") |>
  mutate(diff_debit  = round(debit - coalesce(gl_debit, 0), 2),
         diff_credit = round(credit - coalesce(gl_credit, 0), 2))

tb_check |>
  summarise(tb_debit = sum(debit), gl_debit = sum(gl_debit),
            tb_credit = sum(credit), gl_credit = sum(gl_credit))
```

The totals do not quite agree. Let us find the accounts that differ.

```{r}
tb_check |>
  filter(diff_debit != 0 | diff_credit != 0) |>
  select(account_code, account_name, diff_debit, diff_credit)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
tb_diff <- tb_check |> filter(diff_debit != 0 | diff_credit != 0)
diff_amt <- max(abs(c(tb_diff$diff_debit, tb_diff$diff_credit)))
tb_total <- sum(tb$debit)
```

Two accounts differ, by the same ₹`r inr(diff_amt)`. The trial balance has ₹`r inr(diff_amt)` more debited to `r tb_diff$account_name[tb_diff$diff_debit != 0]`, and the same amount more credited to `r tb_diff$account_name[tb_diff$diff_credit != 0]`. The difference is tiny against total debits of ₹`r crore(tb_total)` crore. But its shape tells a story. It looks like one whole entry, paying an office expense in cash, that is in the books but not in our extract.

### Entries by month

A count of entries by month shows whether any month is missing or thin. Here we count by financial year, period and source.

```{r}
je |>
  count(fy, period, source) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = n)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
p13 <- je |> filter(period == 13)
```

Every month is present, with similar numbers of entries. Period 13 holds `r nrow(p13)` entries, all manual. These are entries dated 31 March 2025 but made after the year had ended. We will look at them closely in @sec-jet-late.

### Gaps in entry numbers

The ERP numbers entries one after another as they are made. A gap in the numbers is an entry we have not received. @sec-gaps showed how to find gaps. `parse_number()` takes the number out of an entry number such as `JE100001`.

```{r}
numbers <- sort(parse_number(je$je_id))
missing_no <- setdiff(seq(min(numbers), max(numbers)), numbers)
missing_no
```

```{r}
je |>
  filter(parse_number(je_id) %in% (missing_no + c(-1, 1))) |>
  select(je_id, entered_at, user_id, amount, narration)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nb <- je |> filter(parse_number(je_id) %in% (missing_no + c(-1, 1)))
```

One number is missing, `JE`r missing_no``. Its neighbours were both entered on `r format(as_date(nb$entered_at[1]), "%d %B %Y")`. So the missing entry was also made that day. Together with the difference in the trial balance, this is a clear lead. An entry of ₹`r inr(diff_amt)` was made, appears in the trial balance, and was left out of the extract. It may have been deleted after the trial balance was printed, or left out by the query. The auditor asks for entry `JE`r missing_no`` and for the reason it is missing, and does not move on until the ledger reconciles.

::: callout-important
## Tests on an incomplete ledger prove nothing

If the extract leaves out entries, the tests in this chapter cannot see them. An entry that someone wished to hide is exactly the entry most likely to be missing. Reconcile the ledger to the trial balance, check the count of entries by month, and look for gaps in the numbers, before running any test. Record the result in the working papers.
:::

## A profile of the ledger {#sec-jet-profile}

Before looking for the unusual, we need to know what is usual. Who posts entries, when, from which source, and to which accounts? Let us begin with the users. We join the entries to the user master.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  left_join(select(users, user_id, department, role), by = "user_id")

je |>
  summarise(entries = n(), value_crore = round(sum(amount) / 1e7, 1),
            .by = c(source, department, role, user_id)) |>
  arrange(source, desc(entries))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
prof <- je |> summarise(entries = n(), .by = c(user_id, department))
acc_entries <- sum(prof$entries[prof$department %in% c("Accounts") & grepl("^ACC", prof$user_id)])
```

The system makes most entries. Among people, the accountants make almost all, `r big(acc_entries)` entries between them. The managers and the General Manager make only a few, and mostly approve. Three users from other departments appear too. They are a payroll officer, a system administrator and a store keeper. We come back to them in @sec-jet-users.

Next, when are entries made? @fig-jet-hours shows the hour of entry, separately for system and manual entries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jet-hours
#| fig-cap: "Entries by hour of entry into the ERP. System entries come in batches, at night and in the morning. Manual entries follow office hours."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
je |>
  mutate(hour = hour(entered_at)) |>
  count(source, hour) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~source, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:23) +
  labs(x = "Hour of entry", y = "Entries") +
  theme_bw()
```

The two sources behave very differently. The billing interface runs at about 11 at night, and bank receipts are imported at about 10 in the morning. Manual entries follow office hours, with a thin tail in the evening and a few dots at night. A test for "entries at night" must therefore treat the two sources separately, or it will flag every storage bill.

Finally, which accounts are used, and how often? Seldom-used accounts deserve attention, because an entry to an account that is rarely touched is harder to explain as routine.

```{r}
gl |>
  summarise(entries = n_distinct(je_id),
            manual = n_distinct(je_id[source == "Manual"]),
            .by = c(account_code, account_name)) |>
  arrange(entries) |>
  head(8)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
acc_use <- gl |> summarise(entries = n_distinct(je_id), .by = c(account_code, account_name)) |> arrange(entries)
n_once <- sum(acc_use$entries == 1)
```

`r n_once` accounts are used only once. Each holds a year-end provision or its expense, booked once a year, so the rarity is expected. Rarity on its own says little. Rare *combinations* of accounts say more, as we will see in @sec-jet-pairs.

## The tests, one characteristic at a time {#sec-jet-tests}

We now run one test for each characteristic in @tbl-jet-characteristics. Each test adds a column to `je` whose name begins with `f_`, for flag. The column is TRUE when the entry has the characteristic. For each test we ask two questions. Why does it matter? And what innocent reasons could produce a hit?

### Entries recorded after the year end {#sec-jet-late}

Entries made after the books are closed, but dated in the closed year, change figures that have already been prepared. Fraudulent entries are often made at this stage, when the result for the year is known and there is pressure to improve it. Our year ended on 31 March 2025.

```{r}
year_end <- as.Date("2025-03-31")

je <- je |>
  mutate(f_postclose = fy == "2024-25" & as_date(entered_at) > year_end)

je |>
  filter(f_postclose) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), value_lakh = round(sum(amount) / 1e5, 1),
            last_entered = max(as_date(entered_at)), .by = c(user_id, role))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pc <- je |> filter(f_postclose) |> summarise(entries = n(), value = sum(amount), .by = user_id)
pc_acm01 <- pc |> filter(user_id == "ACM01")
```

`as_date()` takes the date part of the time stamp. `r sum(je$f_postclose)` entries dated in 2024-25 were made after the year end. Most are innocent. The accountants entered bills of March that arrived late, and the General Manager (Finance) booked the provisions for gratuity and doubtful debts on the basis of reports received in April. These are the normal adjustments of closing. But one manager, `ACM01`, made `r pc_acm01$entries` such entries worth ₹`r lakh(pc_acm01$value)` lakh, far more in value than anyone else. We follow them in @sec-jet-revenue.

### Entries by people who do not normally post {#sec-jet-users}

In a well-run company, only the accounts and finance staff post journal entries. A user from another department who posts entries may be doing someone else's work, may have more access than the role needs, or may be using another person's login. Let us flag manual entries by users outside Accounts and Finance.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_user = source == "Manual" & !department %in% c("Accounts", "Finance"))

je |>
  filter(f_user) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), value_lakh = round(sum(amount) / 1e5, 1),
            .by = c(user_id, department, role))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
fu <- je |> filter(f_user) |> summarise(entries = n(), value = sum(amount), .by = user_id)
```

Three users are found. The payroll officer `HR01` made `r fu$entries[fu$user_id == "HR01"]` small payroll corrections for arrears, a plausible part of the job. The system administrator `ITA02` made `r fu$entries[fu$user_id == "ITA02"]` entries of one rupee, a test and its reversal after an ERP patch. Test entries do not belong in the live ledger, which is itself a point to raise. The store keeper `STR03` made `r fu$entries[fu$user_id == "STR03"]` entries worth ₹`r lakh(fu$value[fu$user_id == "STR03"])` lakh. No ordinary duty of a store keeper explains this. We look closely at `STR03` in @sec-jet-user.

### Entries at night, at weekends and on holidays {#sec-jet-hours}

@sec-lubri-hours looked for approvals made outside office hours. The same test applies to journal entries. A manual entry made at midnight, or on a holiday, is not wrong in itself. But it was made when nobody else was around to see it. We use the hour of `entered_at`, the day of the week, and the list of holidays.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(entered_day = as_date(entered_at),
         entered_hour = hour(entered_at),
         odd_time = entered_hour < 9 | entered_hour >= 19 |
                    wday(entered_day, week_start = 1) >= 6 | entered_day %in% holidays)

je |>
  filter(odd_time) |>
  count(source, user_id, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ot <- je |> filter(odd_time) |> count(source, user_id, sort = TRUE)
ot_sys <- ot$n[ot$source == "System"]
ot_closing <- je |> filter(odd_time, source == "Manual", entered_day %in% as.Date(c("2025-03-29", "2025-03-30")))
```

The system made `r big(ot_sys)` entries at odd times, nearly all of them the nightly billing run. These are innocent, and they would swamp any list. So our flag counts only manual entries.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_offhours = source == "Manual" & odd_time)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ot_m <- je |> filter(f_offhours) |> count(user_id, sort = TRUE)
```

That leaves `r sum(je$f_offhours)` manual entries. `r nrow(ot_closing)` of them were made by the accountants on Saturday 29 and Sunday 30 March 2025, the closing weekend, when the office was open to finish the year. The two test entries of the system administrator were made on a Saturday. The largest group, `r ot_m$n[ot_m$user_id == "STR03"]` entries, belongs to the store keeper `STR03`. The remaining `r ot_m$n[ot_m$user_id == "ACM01"]` belong to `ACM01`, made in the evening and on a Saturday in April 2025.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, time zones and server time

The hour of an entry is only as good as the clock that recorded it. Many ERP systems keep time stamps in UTC, which is five and a half hours behind Indian Standard Time, or in the time zone of a server located elsewhere. Read in the wrong zone, an entry made at 11 in the morning looks like one made at 5:30 in the morning.

```{r}
t_server <- ymd_hms("2025-04-12 05:40:00", tz = "UTC")
with_tz(t_server, "Asia/Kolkata")
```

Before testing hours, ask the IT team how the ERP stores time, and check a few entries whose time you know, such as the nightly billing run. Use `with_tz()` to show a UTC time in Indian time, and `force_tz()` when a time was stored without a zone but is known to be Indian time. @sec-lubridate explains both. Also ask whether `entered_at` is the time of entry or the time of the last change. Some systems overwrite it when an entry is edited.
:::

### Entries approved by their own maker {#sec-jet-self}

An approval is a second pair of eyes. When the maker and the checker are the same person, the control has not operated, whatever the system shows. This is the segregation of duties of @sec-process-sod, checked on every entry. The company's rule allows no self-approval above ₹1 lakh. Let us first see all self-approved entries.

```{r}
je |>
  filter(user_id == approver_id) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), above_1_lakh = sum(amount > 1e5),
            value_lakh = round(sum(amount) / 1e5, 1), .by = c(user_id, role))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sa <- je |> filter(user_id == approver_id) |> summarise(n = n(), big = sum(amount > 1e5), value = sum(amount), .by = user_id)
```

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_self = source == "Manual" & user_id == approver_id & amount > 1e5)
```

`r sum(je$f_self)` entries were approved by their maker above the limit. The manager `ACM02` approved `r sa$big[sa$user_id == "ACM02"]` of their own entries, worth ₹`r lakh(sa$value[sa$user_id == "ACM02"])` lakh in all. The General Manager (Finance) approved `r sa$big[sa$user_id == "FIN01"]` of their own year-end provisions. There may be no one above that officer in the accounts wing, but the rule makes no exception, and provisions of this size would normally need the approval of the Managing Director or the Board. The auditor asks for it. Every hit of this test also shows that the ERP lets a user approve their own entry, which is a weakness in its access rights.

### Entries just below an approval limit {#sec-jet-limit}

@sec-nigrini found bills kept just below a limit. Here the limit is ₹10 lakh, above which the General Manager (Finance) must approve. A person who wishes to avoid that approval may keep entries just under it. Let us look at manual entries between ₹5 lakh and ₹15 lakh in @fig-jet-limit, with the entries of one accountant, `ACC04`, coloured.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jet-limit
#| fig-cap: "Manual entries between ₹5 lakh and ₹15 lakh. The dashed line is the approval limit of ₹10 lakh. Entries pile up just below it, nearly all made by ACC04."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
limit <- 1e6

je |>
  filter(source == "Manual", amount >= 5e5, amount < 1.5e6) |>
  mutate(maker = if_else(user_id == "ACC04", "ACC04", "Others")) |>
  ggplot(aes(amount / 1e5, fill = maker)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = limit / 1e5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("ACC04" = "firebrick", "Others" = "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Amount of entry (₹ lakh)", y = "Entries", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

In an honest ledger, the number of entries falls smoothly as the amount rises. Here a tall bar sits just under the limit. Let us flag manual entries within 5 per cent below the limit, from ₹9.5 lakh up to ₹10 lakh, and count them by user.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_below = source == "Manual" & amount >= 0.95 * limit & amount < limit)

je |>
  filter(f_below) |>
  count(user_id, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
bl <- je |> filter(f_below) |> count(user_id, sort = TRUE)
above_band <- sum(je$source == "Manual" & je$amount >= limit & je$amount < 1.05 * limit)
```

`r bl$n[1]` of the `r sum(bl$n)` entries in this band were made by `r bl$user_id[1]`. In the band of the same width just above the limit, there are only `r above_band` manual entries. An entry of ₹9.8 lakh is ordinary on its own. The finding lies in the pattern of one person, many entries, all just short of the General Manager's approval. The innocent explanation is a run of genuine bills that happen to cost about that much. The auditor checks the bills, the works and the vendors, and asks whether one work was split into several bills.

### Round amounts to suspense and provisions {#sec-jet-round}

@sec-nigrini-round explained why made-up amounts tend to be round. Real bills come from quantities, rates and taxes, so they are seldom exact lakhs. In a ledger, round amounts are most worrying in accounts that hold estimates or unexplained items, such as the suspense account and provisions. Such balances are easy to create and easy to reverse later. Let us find the accounts each entry touches, and flag manual entries to suspense or provision accounts whose amount is an exact multiple of ₹50,000.

```{r}
touches <- gl |>
  summarise(susp_prov = any(account_code %in% c("1601", "2401", "2402", "2403")),
            revenue   = any(account_type == "Income"),
            cash      = any(account_code == "1101"),
            .by = je_id)

je <- je |>
  left_join(touches, by = "je_id") |>
  mutate(f_round = source == "Manual" & susp_prov & amount %% 50000 == 0)

je |>
  filter(f_round) |>
  count(user_id, narration = str_trunc(narration, 45), sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rd <- je |> filter(f_round)
rd_accr <- sum(str_detect(rd$narration, "bill awaited"))
rd_susp <- sum(str_detect(rd$narration, "suspense"))
rd_prov <- sum(rd$narration == "Provision for repairs")
```

`any()` is TRUE if any line of the entry touches the accounts named. `r nrow(rd)` entries are flagged. `r rd_accr` of them are month-end provisions for bills awaited. Provisions are estimates, and estimates are often rounded to a convenient figure, so these are expected. The provision for audit fee is round for the same reason. Two groups are different. The accountant `ACC05` moved `r rd_susp` round sums out of the bank into the suspense account, with the narration "Amount transferred to suspense, to be adjusted". Money leaving the bank to an account that explains nothing needs to be traced. `ACC05` also booked `r rd_prov` round provisions for repairs in March 2025, with no godown and no bill named. They may be genuine estimates, or a way to reduce the year's profit and release it later.

### Narrations that explain nothing {#sec-jet-narration}

Every entry should say why it was made. An entry with no narration, or with a word such as "adj", cannot be understood without going back to the person who made it. @sec-text-je used a dictionary of red-flag words, combined with other flags, on the narrations of journal entries. Here we add a simpler test. It looks for narrations that are blank, too short to mean anything, or one of a few phrases known to explain nothing. Let us try it on five narrations first.

```{r}
vague <- c("adj", "adjustment", "as per instructions", "ok", "jv", "na", "misc")

tibble(narration = c("", "adj", "Being bill no 512 of vendor V-020 for electricity",
                     "..", "As per instructions")) |>
  mutate(narr = str_to_lower(str_squish(narration)),
         vague = narr %in% vague | !str_detect(narr, "[a-z]{4,}"))
```

`str_squish()` removes extra spaces, and `str_to_lower()` makes the case uniform. The pattern `[a-z]{4,}` means "a word of at least four letters". A narration without any such word, like "adj" or "..", cannot say much. Now for all manual entries.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(narr = str_to_lower(str_squish(narration)),
         f_narration = source == "Manual" & (narr %in% vague | !str_detect(narr, "[a-z]{4,}")))

je |>
  filter(f_narration) |>
  count(user_id, narration, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nr <- je |> filter(f_narration)
nr_petty <- sum(nr$narration == "" & nr$amount < 10000)
nr_acc05 <- sum(nr$user_id == "ACC05")
```

`r nrow(nr)` entries are flagged. `r nr_petty` of them are small petty cash payments keyed in without a narration, a lapse of care rather than a sign of fraud. `r nr_acc05` belong to `ACC05`, the accountant who also appears in the round-amount test. For a deeper reading of narrations, with dictionaries and word frequencies, see @sec-text-je and @sec-text.

### The same entry posted twice {#sec-jet-dup}

An entry posted twice doubles an expense, a liability or, worse, a payment. @sec-dup taught the "same-same-same" test. For journal entries, "the same" means the same accounts, the same amounts on the same side, and the same narration. We first make a **signature** of each entry, a single piece of text listing its accounts and net amounts in a fixed order.

```{r}
signatures <- gl |>
  arrange(je_id, account_code) |>
  summarise(sig     = paste(account_code, round(debit - credit, 2), collapse = "|"),
            rev_sig = paste(account_code, round(credit - debit, 2), collapse = "|"),
            .by = je_id)

je <- je |>
  left_join(signatures, by = "je_id")

je |>
  select(je_id, sig, rev_sig) |>
  head(3)
```

A debit shows as a positive number and a credit as a negative one. Two entries with the same signature move the same amounts through the same accounts. We will use `rev_sig`, the signature with the signs turned round, in the next test. Now let us find entries whose signature and narration match another entry posted within seven days.

```{r}
near_dups <- je |>
  arrange(sig, narration, posting_date) |>
  mutate(gap_before = as.numeric(posting_date - lag(posting_date)),
         gap_after  = as.numeric(lead(posting_date) - posting_date),
         .by = c(sig, narration)) |>
  filter(gap_before <= 7 | gap_after <= 7)

near_dups |>
  count(source, small = amount < 10000)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
nd_small <- sum(near_dups$amount < 10000)
```

`r nd_small` of the matches are below ₹10,000. They are petty cash payments of the same round sum, such as ₹1,000 for courier charges, made a few days apart. That is normal. Let us keep entries of ₹10,000 or more.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_dup = je_id %in% near_dups$je_id[near_dups$amount >= 10000])

je |>
  filter(f_dup) |>
  select(je_id, posting_date, entered_at, user_id, amount, narration)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dp <- je |> filter(f_dup)
```

Only one pair is left. The same bill of vendor V-088, ₹`r inr(dp$amount[1])`, was posted on `r format(dp$posting_date[1], "%d %B")` and again on `r format(dp$posting_date[2], "%d %B %Y")`, by the same accountant. The auditor checks whether the vendor was paid twice, and whether the second entry has been reversed since.

### Entries reversed soon after the year end {#sec-jet-reversed}

An entry booked at the year end and reversed soon after the new year begins had an effect only on the year-end figures. That is the purpose of genuine accruals, which are reversed when the actual bill arrives. It is also the mark of window dressing, where income or assets are shown at the year end and quietly taken back later. The reversal of an entry has the opposite signature, so we join the entries of March 2025 to entries of April and May 2025 whose `rev_sig` matches.

```{r}
march <- je |>
  filter(fy == "2024-25", posting_date >= as.Date("2025-03-01")) |>
  select(je_id, posting_date, user_id, amount, narration, sig)

later <- je |>
  filter(posting_date > year_end) |>
  select(rev_id = je_id, rev_date = posting_date, rev_user = user_id, rev_sig)

reversed <- march |>
  inner_join(later, by = c("sig" = "rev_sig"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  summarise(first_reversal = min(rev_date), rev_user = first(rev_user),
            .by = c(je_id, posting_date, user_id, amount, narration)) |>
  mutate(days_to_reverse = as.numeric(first_reversal - posting_date))

reversed |>
  select(je_id, user_id, amount, days_to_reverse, rev_user, narration)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rv <- reversed |> mutate(auto = rev_user == "SYSTEM")
rv_auto <- sum(rv$auto)
rv_man <- rv |> filter(!auto)
```

`relationship = "many-to-many"` tells `inner_join()` that one entry may match more than one reversal. This happens when two entries share an amount by chance, so we keep only the first reversal of each entry. `r nrow(rv)` entries of March were reversed in April or May. `r rv_auto` are provisions for bills awaited, reversed automatically by the system on 1 April. That is the normal cycle of accruals. The other `r nrow(rv_man)` are the storage income entries of `ACM01`, reversed by hand after `r min(rv_man$days_to_reverse)` to `r max(rv_man$days_to_reverse)` days.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_reversed = je_id %in% reversed$je_id)
```

### Manual entries to revenue and cash {#sec-jet-revcash}

Revenue is often the target of fraud in financial reporting, and cash is the asset most easily taken. In our company, revenue is recorded by the billing interface, and cash in hand is used only for petty expenses. So a manual entry to revenue, or a large manual entry to cash, needs a reason. We flag manual entries that touch any income account, and manual entries to cash in hand above ₹50,000.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_rev_cash = source == "Manual" & (revenue | (cash & amount > 50000)))

je |>
  filter(f_rev_cash) |>
  count(revenue, cash, narration = str_trunc(narration, 50), sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rc <- je |> filter(f_rev_cash)
```

`r nrow(rc)` entries are flagged. Most are small miscellaneous income, such as the sale of tender forms and scrap gunny bags, and the quarterly interest on deposits. These are expected. The rest are the storage income entries of `ACM01` and their reversals, and three payments in cash to a contractor, which the next section looks at.

::: callout-warning
## Caution, a flag is a lead

- **Every test has innocent hits.** Accruals are round, closing weekends are worked, late bills are entered in April, and provisions are reversed. Expect most flags to have a good reason, and read the reason before writing anything.
- **System entries trigger tests innocently.** The billing run is posted at night, depreciation is the same round sum every month, and auto-reversals look exactly like window dressing. Test system entries separately, and test the interface itself, not each entry it makes.
- **A test can only see what is in the data.** An entry made under someone else's login looks like that person's entry. A time stamp in the wrong zone moves every entry. The tests point to entries. Documents, logs and people explain them.
:::

## Rare account combinations {#sec-jet-pairs}

Each entry moves value from some accounts to others. A bill moves it from trade payables to an expense. A receipt moves it from receivables to the bank. In any organisation, most entries follow a small number of such routes. A route used only once or twice in a year is unusual by definition. It may be an honest one-off, such as capitalising a finished building. It may also be an entry that no routine process would make.

Let us see the idea on the two tiny entries from @sec-jet-entries. We pair each debited account with each credited account of the same entry.

```{r}
tiny_dr <- tiny |> filter(debit > 0) |> distinct(je_id, dr = account_code)
tiny_cr <- tiny |> filter(credit > 0) |> distinct(je_id, cr = account_code)
inner_join(tiny_dr, tiny_cr, by = "je_id")
```

The bill gives two pairs, repairs with payables and GST input with payables. The receipt gives one, bank with receivables. Now let us do the same for every entry, and count how many entries use each pair.

```{r}
pairs <- gl |>
  filter(debit > 0) |>
  distinct(je_id, dr = account_code) |>
  inner_join(gl |> filter(credit > 0) |> distinct(je_id, cr = account_code),
             by = "je_id", relationship = "many-to-many")

pair_counts <- pairs |>
  count(dr, cr, name = "entries") |>
  left_join(select(coa, dr = account_code, debit_account = account_name), by = "dr") |>
  left_join(select(coa, cr = account_code, credit_account = account_name), by = "cr")

pair_counts |>
  filter(entries < 10) |>
  arrange(entries) |>
  select(debit_account, credit_account, entries)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rare <- pair_counts |> filter(entries < 10)
n_pairs <- nrow(pair_counts)
adv_prov <- pairs |> filter(dr == "1301", cr == "2401") |> left_join(select(je, je_id, f_narration), by = "je_id")
```

There are `r n_pairs` pairs in all, and `r nrow(rare)` are used in fewer than ten entries over the fourteen months. Most are easy to explain. Gratuity, doubtful debts and audit fee are provided once a year. Godowns are capitalised when they are finished. Interest comes each quarter. The reversal of the test entry of the system administrator gives a pair of its own. Four pairs stand out.

- **Capital work-in-progress paid from cash in hand.** Contractors are always paid through the bank. Three payments in cash to a contractor, each around ₹2 lakh, avoid the bank trail.
- **Suspense account debited, bank credited.** Genuine suspense entries go the other way, parking unidentified receipts until they are cleared. Here money leaves the bank for the suspense account. These are the round transfers of `ACC05`.
- **Advances to staff debited, provision for expenses credited.** An advance is paid from the bank, not out of a provision. `r if (all(adv_prov$f_narration)) paste0("All ", nrow(adv_prov), " such entries") else paste(nrow(adv_prov), "entries")` have narrations that explain nothing.
- **Storage charges debited, receivables credited.** Storage income is never reduced in the normal course. This route is used only by the six reversals of `ACM01` in May 2025.

```{r}
je <- je |>
  mutate(f_rare = je_id %in% semi_join(pairs, rare, by = c("dr", "cr"))$je_id)
```

`semi_join()` keeps the pairs of entries that appear in `rare`, and we flag those entries. The threshold of ten is a judgement. A larger organisation, or a longer period, would need a higher one.

::: callout-note
## Rare pairs and association rules

Counting pairs is the simplest form of the idea behind association rules (@sec-apriori). There, we looked for items that often go together. Here we turn the question round, and look for accounts that seldom go together. With many lines per entry, the same approach can look at sets of three or more accounts, and a measure such as lift can show whether a pair is rarer than the popularity of its two accounts would suggest.
:::

## Combining the tests into a risk score {#sec-jet-score}

We now have eleven flags. An entry with one flag is common. An entry with several is not. As in @sec-tenderflags-cri and @sec-text-je, we add the flags into a score. Here we give each flag a weight, because the tests are not equally strong. The weights below were fixed by the audit team before looking at the results, with a reason for each.

| Flag | Weight | Reason |
|-----------------|--------|----------------------------------------|
| `f_self` | 3 | Breaks a control the company itself has set |
| `f_dup` | 3 | If genuine, an expense or a payment is counted twice |
| `f_postclose` | 2 | Changes figures after the books were closed |
| `f_user` | 2 | Outside the duties of the person's role |
| `f_below` | 2 | Suggests that an approval is being avoided |
| `f_round` | 2 | Round estimates in accounts that are easy to reverse later |
| `f_rare` | 2 | A route that no routine process uses |
| `f_reversed` | 2 | An effect only on the year-end figures |
| `f_offhours` | 1 | Common and often innocent, but worth adding |
| `f_narration` | 1 | A lapse of care more often than a sign of fraud |
| `f_rev_cash` | 1 | Mostly routine income, weak on its own |

: Weights given to each test {#tbl-jet-weights}

The same weights in R, and the score for each entry.

```{r}
weights <- c(f_self = 3, f_dup = 3, f_postclose = 2, f_user = 2, f_below = 2,
             f_round = 2, f_rare = 2, f_reversed = 2, f_offhours = 1,
             f_narration = 1, f_rev_cash = 1)

scores <- je |>
  select(je_id, all_of(names(weights))) |>
  pivot_longer(-je_id, names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
  summarise(flags = sum(raised),
            score = sum(raised * weights[flag]),
            which = paste(flag[raised], collapse = ", "),
            .by = je_id) |>
  left_join(select(je, je_id, source, user_id, posting_date, amount, narration), by = "je_id")

scores |>
  count(source, score)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sc_dist <- scores |> count(source, score)
n_zero <- sum(scores$score == 0)
n_high <- sum(scores$score >= 3)
```

`pivot_longer()` turns the flag columns into rows, one per entry and flag. `weights[flag]` looks up the weight of each flag by its name. `r big(n_zero)` entries raise no flag at all, including every system entry. Only `r n_high` entries score 3 or more. Here are the highest.

```{r}
scores |>
  arrange(desc(score), desc(amount)) |>
  select(je_id, user_id, amount, score, which) |>
  head(10)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
top10 <- scores |> arrange(desc(score), desc(amount)) |> head(10)
```

At the top are the two provisions of the General Manager (Finance), each scoring `r top10$score[1]`. They were self-approved, made after the close, and posted to accounts used once a year. They are probably genuine, but their size alone would justify a look at the papers behind them. Next come the storage income entries of `ACM01`.

### Selecting entries for examination {#sec-jet-select}

The score ranks entries. It does not choose them by itself. A common approach has two parts. First, examine **every** entry above a cut-off, chosen in advance. We use a score of 3 or more. Second, add a **random sample** of the remaining manual entries. The sample gives coverage. It tests the entries that raised no flag, and so tests the tests themselves. If the sample finds problems the flags missed, the tests need to be widened. @sec-sampling explains random sampling, and @sec-stratified how to spread a sample across groups.

```{r}
high_risk <- scores |>
  filter(score >= 3)

set.seed(2025)
random_pick <- scores |>
  filter(source == "Manual", score < 3) |>
  slice_sample(n = 25)

selection <- bind_rows(
  high_risk |> mutate(reason = "Score of 3 or more"),
  random_pick |> mutate(reason = "Random sample")
)

selection |>
  count(reason)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
sel_planted <- high_risk |> inner_join(planted, by = "je_id")
pl_all <- planted |> filter(case != "Missing") |> left_join(scores, by = "je_id")
miss <- pl_all |> filter(score < 3) |> count(case)
rand_planted <- random_pick |> inner_join(planted, by = "je_id")
miss_below <- miss$n[miss$case == "4 Below limit"]
miss_prov <- miss$n[miss$case == "5 Round to provision"]
miss_narr <- miss$n[miss$case == "7 Narration"]
miss_store <- miss$n[miss$case == "2 Store keeper"]
```

The selection has `r nrow(high_risk)` high-risk entries and `r nrow(random_pick)` random ones. Since we planted the cases, we can check how well the score did. Of the `r nrow(high_risk)` high-risk entries, `r nrow(sel_planted)` are planted. The other `r nrow(high_risk) - nrow(sel_planted)` are genuine. They are the quarterly interest entries, which credit revenue through a rare pair, the two test entries, a few provisions of March that were round and then reversed, and the year-end provisions of the finance team. The auditor will clear them quickly from the documents.

The score also missed some planted entries, and it is worth being honest about why.

- **All `r miss_below` bills just below the limit score only 2.** Each is ordinary on its own. The scheme shows only in the count by user in @sec-jet-limit.
- **The `r miss_prov` round provisions for repairs score 2.** They look like the many genuine month-end provisions.
- **`r miss_narr` of the 12 vague narrations score 1**, because they raise no other flag.
- **`r miss_store` of the store keeper's entries score 2**, because they were made in office hours.

`r if (nrow(rand_planted) == 0) "None of these fell in the random sample, which is what we should expect when a few dozen entries hide among thousands." else paste0("By chance, ", nrow(rand_planted), " of the missed entries fell in the random sample. We cannot rely on such luck.")` So the selection should have a third part. Where a test shows a **pattern** rather than a single entry, such as one user's cluster below the limit, the auditor selects the whole pattern. The score is for entries. Patterns are found by reading the results of each test, by user and by account, as we did above.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip, recording the selection

Save the selection with the reason for each entry, the weights, the cut-off and the seed of the random sample, in the working papers. Anyone can then run the code again and get the same list. If the weights are changed after the results are seen, say so, and keep both versions.
:::

## Audit use case, a year-end revenue boost {#sec-jet-revenue}

Three tests pointed at the same six entries of `ACM01`. They were made after the year end, they credit revenue, and they were reversed within weeks. Let us put them together with their reversals.

```{r}
boost <- reversed |>
  filter(user_id == "ACM01") |>
  left_join(select(je, je_id, entered_at, approver_id), by = "je_id") |>
  select(je_id, posting_date, entered_at, approver_id, amount, first_reversal, days_to_reverse)

boost
```

```{r}
#| include: false
b_total <- sum(boost$amount)
storage_fy <- gl |>
  filter(fy == "2024-25", account_code == "3101") |>
  summarise(net = sum(credit) - sum(debit)) |> pull(net)
b_share <- 100 * b_total / storage_fy
b_entered <- range(as_date(boost$entered_at))
```

All six entries are dated 31 March 2025, but were keyed in between `r day(b_entered[1])` and `r day(b_entered[2])` `r format(b_entered[2], "%B %Y")`. Each was approved by the General Manager (Finance), because each was above ₹10 lakh. So the approval control operated, and the entries still went through. This is what override of controls looks like. Together they add ₹`r crore(b_total)` crore to storage charges.

How do these entries compare with genuine storage bills? Every genuine bill comes from the billing interface and carries GST, because storage is a taxable service. Let us check which entries crediting storage charges also have a GST line.

```{r}
gl |>
  filter(fy == "2024-25") |>
  summarise(storage = any(account_code == "3101" & credit > 0),
            gst = any(account_code == "2302"),
            .by = c(je_id, source, user_id)) |>
  filter(storage) |>
  count(source, user_id, gst)
```

Every system bill has a GST line. None of the six manual entries does. If the income were real, GST would be due on it. Its absence suggests that no bills were ever meant to be raised, which the reversals in May confirm. The narration of the reversals, "Rectification of entry dated 31.03.2025", says nothing about why.

What was the effect on the accounts? Let us compare the storage charges of 2024-25 with and without these entries.

```{r}
tibble(
  item = c("Storage charges as per ledger", "Entries of ACM01 booked after year end",
           "Storage charges without them"),
  crore = round(c(storage_fy, b_total, storage_fy - b_total) / 1e7, 2)
)
```

The six entries overstate storage charges for 2024-25 by `r round(b_share, 1)` per cent. Profit before tax is overstated by the same ₹`r crore(b_total)` crore, because no cost was booked against them. Trade receivables at 31 March 2025 are overstated by the same amount. In 2025-26, the reversals will reduce storage income by ₹`r crore(b_total)` crore, so the boost moves profit from one year to the other. @fig-jet-revenue shows the storage charges month by month.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jet-revenue
#| fig-cap: "Storage charges by month of posting, net of reversals, in ₹ crore. March 2025 is lifted by the entries of ACM01, and May 2025 is lowered by their reversal."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "85%"
gl |>
  filter(account_code == "3101") |>
  mutate(month = floor_date(posting_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(crore = (sum(credit) - sum(debit)) / 1e7, .by = month) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, crore)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %y", date_breaks = "2 months") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Storage charges (₹ crore)") +
  theme_bw()
```

`floor_date()` from `lubridate` turns each date into the first day of its month, so that entries can be totalled by month.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Ask for the documents.** For each entry, ask for the bills, the depositors and the stock registers that support the income. Storage income must match goods actually stored.
2. **Ask about the approval.** Ask the General Manager (Finance) what was seen before approving, in the middle of April, entries dated 31 March.
3. **Look at the ERP logs.** Check when and from which computer the entries were made, whether period 12 was reopened, and whether the reversals came after the accounts were adopted.
4. **Ask for a written explanation**, and compare it with the management representation letter. If management represents that all income is genuine, the reversals contradict it.
5. **Word the observation carefully.** State the facts. Six entries, their dates of entry, the absence of bills and GST, the reversal in May, and the effect of ₹`r crore(b_total)` crore on revenue, profit and receivables. Recommend correction of the accounts and a review of who can post to revenue after the year end. Leave intent to the competent authority.

## Audit use case, a user who should not be posting {#sec-jet-user}

The store keeper `STR03` appeared in two tests, as a user outside accounts and for entries at odd times. Let us list every entry.

```{r}
store <- je |>
  filter(user_id == "STR03") |>
  mutate(day = wday(entered_at, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
         holiday = entered_day %in% holidays,
         vendor = str_extract(narration, "V-\\d+")) |>
  select(je_id, entered_at, day, holiday, approver_id, vendor, amount)

store
```

```{r}
#| include: false
st_hour <- hour(store$entered_at)
st_night <- sum(st_hour < 9 | st_hour >= 19)
st_hol <- sum(store$holiday)
st_week <- sum(store$day %in% c("Sat", "Sun") & !store$holiday)
st_total <- sum(store$amount)
```

`str_extract()` with the pattern `V-\\d+` picks out the vendor code from the narration. The picture is clear. All `r nrow(store)` entries are bills of one vendor, `r unique(store$vendor)`, for fumigation chemicals, worth ₹`r lakh(st_total)` lakh. `r st_night` were entered before 9 in the morning or after 7 in the evening, `r st_hol` on gazetted holidays, and `r st_week` more on Saturdays. All were approved by the same manager, `r unique(store$approver_id)`.

Has anyone else ever posted a bill of this vendor? And was it paid?

```{r}
je |>
  filter(str_detect(narration, "V-217")) |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(str_detect(narration, "^Payment"), "Payment", "Bill")) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), value_lakh = round(sum(amount) / 1e5, 1),
            .by = c(kind, user_id))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
v217 <- je |> filter(str_detect(narration, "V-217")) |> mutate(kind = if_else(str_detect(narration, "^Payment"), "Payment", "Bill"))
v_paid <- sum(v217$amount[v217$kind == "Payment"])
```
