No accountant ever booked a bill of `V-217`. Every bill came from the store keeper, and the accountants then paid them in the normal course, ₹`r lakh(v_paid)` lakh in all. This is a failure of **segregation of duties**, as in @sec-process-sod. The store keeper records the receipt of chemicals in the stores. If the same person can also book the vendor's bill, one person can create both the proof of supply and the liability to pay. The approver is the only check left, and the same manager `ACM02` also approved their own entries in @sec-jet-self.

The user master tells us what the role should allow.

```{r}
users |>
  filter(user_id %in% c("STR03", "ACM02"))
```

A store keeper has no reason to hold rights to post journal entries. Either the rights were given by mistake, or someone else used the store keeper's login, perhaps at night when it was not in use. The pattern of times suggests the second possibility, but only the logs can show it.

### What the auditor does next

1. **Ask how the access was given.** Get the rights of `STR03` from the ERP, and the approval under which posting rights were granted.
2. **Check the ERP logs.** Find the computer and login session of each entry, and compare the times with the store keeper's attendance and leave. Entries made on Republic Day need explaining.
3. **Verify the supply.** Match each bill with the goods received note, the stock register of chemicals and the fumigation records of the godowns.
4. **Look at the vendor.** Check the registration, address, GST number and bank account of `V-217`, and any link to staff, as in @sec-dup and @sec-netaudit.
5. **Talk to the people.** Ask the store keeper and the approving manager, separately and on record, about the entries.
6. **Word the observation carefully.** Report the access failure as a control weakness in any case. Report the bills as unsupported only if the documents are missing. Leave any conclusion about who made the entries to the investigation that follows.

## A suggested workflow

1. **Get the full ledger extract**, with user, approver, source, posting date and time of entry, the user master, the chart of accounts, the holidays and the trial balance.
2. **Check completeness.** Every entry balances, the ledger agrees with the trial balance, every month is present, and there are no gaps in the numbers. Resolve every difference before going further.
3. **Make one row per entry**, and add the department of each user and the accounts each entry touches.
4. **Profile the ledger.** Who posts, when, from which source, and to which accounts. Note what is routine.
5. **Run one test per characteristic.** Late entries, unusual users, odd times, self-approval, amounts below limits, round amounts, vague narrations, duplicates, reversals, and manual entries to revenue and cash. Look at the results of each test by user and by account.
6. **Count account pairs** and look at the rare ones.
7. **Combine the flags into a score**, with weights and a cut-off fixed in advance, and written down.
8. **Select entries.** All high scores, every pattern found by a test, and a random sample of the rest.
9. **Examine the selected entries** with documents, approvals, ERP logs and explanations from the people concerned, and report facts.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- Journal entries are where controls can be overridden. Standards on auditing require them to be tested, especially at the period end.
- Reconcile the ledger to the trial balance and look for gaps before any test. A test on an incomplete ledger proves nothing.
- Know what is routine before looking for the unusual. System entries, accruals and closing work trigger many tests innocently.
- Each test answers one question. Read its results by user and by account, because some schemes show only as patterns.
- A score ranks entries. Fix its weights in advance, examine all high scores, and add a random sample for coverage.
- A flag is a lead. Documents, logs and people decide whether it is a finding.
:::

## Where next

The date and time functions used here are explained in @sec-lubridate, and checks on approvals outside office hours in @sec-lubri-hours. Round amounts and amounts below limits are treated more fully in @sec-nigrini, and Benford's law, which can also be applied to the amounts of journal entries, in @sec-benford. @sec-dup covers duplicates, including near matches. The narrations of entries can be read with the methods of @sec-text-je. Many rules of this chapter, such as the approval limits, can also be written as a rule book, as in @sec-validate. Statistical outliers among amounts or users are found with the methods of @sec-anomaly. The risk score follows the same logic as the index for tenders in @sec-tenderflags-cri, and the random part of the selection uses @sec-sampling.

## Try it yourself {#sec-jet-exercises}

These exercises use the tables `gl`, `je`, `users`, `pair_counts` and `scores` of this chapter. Try each one before you open the solution.

1.  **Users outside their period of service.** Join `je` with the joining and leaving dates in `users`. Are there any manual entries made before a user joined or after a user left?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_service <- je |>
      filter(source == "Manual") |>
      left_join(select(users, user_id, joined, left), by = "user_id") |>
      filter(entered_day < joined | (!is.na(left) & entered_day > left))
    nrow(ex_service)
    ```
    ```{r}
    ex_service |>
      select(je_id, posting_date, entered_at, user_id, amount, narration)
    ```
    There is `r nrow(ex_service)` such entry. It is a bill dated `r format(ex_service$posting_date[1], "%d %B %Y")`, keyed in on `r day(ex_service$entered_day[1])` `r format(ex_service$entered_day[1], "%B %Y")` under the login of `r ex_service$user_id[1]`, who left on 31 December 2024. Perhaps a colleague finished the work with the old login, or the date of leaving in the master is wrong. Either way, a login that should have been closed was still in use. The auditor asks the IT team when it was disabled.
    :::

2.  **Late at night.** Count the manual entries made between 9 in the evening and 6 in the morning, by user. Who made the most?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_night <- je |>
      filter(source == "Manual", entered_hour >= 21 | entered_hour < 6) |>
      count(user_id, sort = TRUE)
    ex_night
    ```
    `r ex_night$user_id[1]` made `r ex_night$n[1]` entries late at night. `r if (nrow(ex_night) == 1) "No other user made any." else "Other users made only a few."` Even the accountants working over the closing weekend did not work at night.
    :::

3.  **Storage income by month.** Using `gl`, find the net storage charges (account `3101`) for each month of 2024-25, in ₹ crore. How does March 2025 compare with the average of the other eleven months?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_month <- gl |>
      filter(fy == "2024-25", account_code == "3101") |>
      mutate(month = floor_date(posting_date, "month")) |>
      summarise(crore = round((sum(credit) - sum(debit)) / 1e7, 2), .by = month) |>
      arrange(month)
    ex_month
    ex_march <- ex_month$crore[ex_month$month == as.Date("2025-03-01")]
    ex_other <- mean(ex_month$crore[ex_month$month != as.Date("2025-03-01")])
    ```
    March 2025 shows ₹`r ex_march` crore, against an average of ₹`r round(ex_other, 2)` crore for the other months. The difference is roughly the six entries of `ACM01`. A month-by-month view of revenue is a quick first check before any journal entry test.
    :::

4.  **A wider rare-pair limit.** Change the limit for rare pairs from fewer than 10 entries to fewer than 20. Which pairs are added, and are they suspicious?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_pairs <- pair_counts |>
      filter(entries >= 10, entries < 20) |>
      select(debit_account, credit_account, entries)
    ex_pairs
    ```
    `r nrow(ex_pairs)` pairs are added. They are monthly postings, such as salary and statutory payments, depreciation and security services, made once a month for fourteen months. They are routine, which shows that a limit set too high fills the list with monthly entries.
    :::

5.  **A different weight.** The audit team decides that an entry by a user outside accounts should weigh 3 instead of 2. Recompute the score and count how many entries now score 3 or more, and how many of them were made by `STR03`.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_weights <- weights
    ex_weights["f_user"] <- 3
    ex_scores <- je |>
      select(je_id, user_id, all_of(names(ex_weights))) |>
      pivot_longer(-c(je_id, user_id), names_to = "flag", values_to = "raised") |>
      summarise(score = sum(raised * ex_weights[flag]), .by = c(je_id, user_id))
    ex_high <- ex_scores |> filter(score >= 3)
    nrow(ex_high)
    sum(ex_high$user_id == "STR03")
    ```
    `r nrow(ex_high)` entries now score 3 or more, against `r nrow(high_risk)` before. All `r sum(ex_high$user_id == "STR03")` entries of `STR03` are now selected, and so are the payroll corrections and the test entries. A change of weight changes the list. That is why the weights are fixed and recorded before the results are seen.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `summarise(.by = )` | dplyr | Turns lines into entries, and totals the ledger by account |
| `left_join()`, `inner_join()`, `semi_join()` | dplyr | Joins the trial balance, user master and accounts, matches entries with their reversals, and keeps rare pairs |
| `coalesce()` | dplyr | Treats an account missing from the ledger as zero |
| `lag()`, `lead()` | dplyr | Days to the previous and next entry with the same signature |
| `any()` | base R | Whether any line of an entry touches an account |
| `parse_number()` | readr | Takes the number out of an entry number, to look for gaps |
| `setdiff()`, `seq()` | base R | Numbers missing from a sequence |
| `as_date()`, `hour()`, `wday()` | lubridate | Date, hour and day of the week of the time of entry |
| `with_tz()`, `ymd_hms()` | lubridate | Shows a time stamp stored in UTC in Indian time |
| `floor_date()` | lubridate | First day of the month, to total entries by month |
| `str_squish()`, `str_to_lower()`, `str_detect()`, `str_extract()` | stringr | Cleans narrations, finds vague ones, and picks out vendor codes |
| `pivot_longer()`, `pivot_wider()` | tidyr | Flags into rows for the score, and sources into columns for display |
| `slice_sample()` | dplyr | Random sample of the remaining entries |
| `geom_col()`, `geom_histogram()`, `geom_vline()` | ggplot2 | Entries by hour and month, and amounts near the approval limit |
